context: Give an example of a metal which
stem: is a liquid at room temperature.
solution:
**Mercury.**

Every other metal is a solid at room temperature; mercury is the one exception, which is why it is the metal used in thermometers.
groundedIn: §3.1.1 Metals, with Activity 3.2 and Activity 3.5 — the book records that all metals except mercury are solids at room temperature, that sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife, and that the best conductors of heat are silver and copper while lead and mercury are comparatively poor.

subtopic: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
stem: Explain the meanings of malleable and ductile.
solution:
**Malleable.** A substance is malleable if it can be **beaten into thin sheets** without breaking. Metals are malleable as a class, and **gold and silver are the most malleable** of them.

**Ductile.** A substance is ductile if it can be **drawn into thin wires**. **Gold is the most ductile metal** — a wire about 2 km long can be drawn from a single gram of it.

It is because metals are both malleable and ductile that they can be given whatever shape a use calls for.
groundedIn: §3.1.1 Metals, with Activity 3.3 (malleability) and Activity 3.4 (ductility), which give both definitions and both superlatives.

stem: Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil?
solution:
Sodium is **so reactive towards oxygen that it catches fire if left in the open**. Potassium behaves the same way.

Kerosene keeps air and moisture off the metal surface, so the sodium can neither react with the oxygen of the air nor react violently with water vapour. Storing it under kerosene both protects the metal and **prevents accidental fires**.
groundedIn: §3.2.1 What happens when Metals are burnt in Air?, which states that potassium and sodium react so vigorously that they catch fire if kept in the open and are therefore kept immersed in kerosene oil.

context: Write equations for the reactions of
stem: iron with steam
solution:
Iron does not react with cold or hot water, but it **does react with steam**, giving the oxide and hydrogen:

\(3\text{Fe}(s) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightarrow \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(s) + 4\text{H}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §3.2.2 What happens when Metals react with Water?, with Activity 3.10 and Fig. 3.3 — metals react with water to give a metal oxide (or hydroxide) and hydrogen, and the section gives the potassium, sodium, calcium and steam reactions explicitly.

context: Write equations for the reactions of
stem: calcium and potassium with water
solution:
**Calcium with water.** The reaction is less violent than potassium's — the heat evolved is not enough for the hydrogen to catch fire:

\(\text{Ca}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

The calcium starts floating, because bubbles of hydrogen stick to its surface.

**Potassium with water.** Violent and strongly exothermic — the hydrogen evolved catches fire at once:

\(2\text{K}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{KOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g) + \text{heat energy}\)
groundedIn: §3.2.2 What happens when Metals react with Water?, with Activity 3.10 and Fig. 3.3 — metals react with water to give a metal oxide (or hydroxide) and hydrogen, and the section gives the potassium, sodium, calcium and steam reactions explicitly.

Samples of four metals A, B, C and D were taken and added to the following solutions one by one. The results obtained have been tabulated as follows.

| Metal | Iron(II) sulphate | Copper(II) sulphate | Zinc sulphate | Silver nitrate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | No reaction | Displacement | — | — |
| B | Displacement | — | No reaction | — |
| C | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | Displacement |
| D | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction |

(A dash marks a cell the book leaves blank.) Use the table above to answer the following questions about metals A, B, C and D.
stem: Which is the most reactive metal?
solution:
**B is the most reactive.**

Read each result as a comparison:

- **B** displaces iron from iron(II) sulphate, so **B is more reactive than iron**. It does not react with zinc sulphate, so it is **less reactive than zinc**. That places B between zinc and iron.
- **A** does not displace iron, so it is **less reactive than iron**, but it does displace copper, so it is **more reactive than copper**.
- **C** displaces only silver, so it sits **below copper and above silver**.
- **D** displaces nothing at all, not even silver, so it is **the least reactive**.

B is the only metal that outranks iron, so B is the most reactive of the four.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? and §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2 — if metal A displaces metal B from its solution it is the more reactive of the two, and Table 3.2 orders K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

stem: What would you observe if B is added to a solution of Copper(II) sulphate?
solution:
**A displacement reaction takes place.** B is more reactive than iron, and iron is more reactive than copper, so B is more reactive than copper and displaces it from the solution.

What you would see:

- The **blue colour of the copper(II) sulphate solution fades**, as the copper ions leave it.
- A **reddish-brown deposit of copper** collects on the surface of B.

stem: Arrange the metals A, B, C and D in the order of decreasing reactivity.
solution:
**B \(>\) A \(>\) C \(>\) D**

- **B** is above iron (it displaces iron).
- **A** is below iron but above copper (it fails with iron, succeeds with copper).
- **C** is below copper but above silver (it fails with copper, succeeds with silver).
- **D** fails even with silver nitrate, so it is below silver and least reactive of all.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? and §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2 — if metal A displaces metal B from its solution it is the more reactive of the two, and Table 3.2 orders K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

stem: Which gas is produced when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a reactive metal? Write the chemical reaction when iron reacts with dilute H₂SO₄.
solution:
**Hydrogen gas** is produced. A metal above hydrogen in the activity series displaces it from a dilute acid:

Metal + Dilute acid \(\rightarrow\) Salt + Hydrogen

**Iron with dilute sulphuric acid:**

\(\text{Fe}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Dilute acid gives iron(II) sulphate, so the iron here is in the \(+2\) state.
groundedIn: §3.2.3 What happens when Metals react with Acids?, which gives the general form metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen, with Activity 3.11 and Table 3.2 for which metals lie above hydrogen.

stem: What would you observe when zinc is added to a solution of iron(II) sulphate? Write the chemical reaction that takes place.
solution:
**Zinc is more reactive than iron**, so it displaces iron from the solution.

What you would see:

- The **pale green colour of the iron(II) sulphate solution fades**, since the iron ions are leaving it.
- A **greyish-black deposit of iron** collects on the zinc.

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{FeSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{ZnSO}_4(aq) + \text{Fe}(s)\)

This is a **displacement reaction**.
groundedIn: §3.2.4 How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts? with Activity 3.12 and Fig. 3.4 — a reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution — and Table 3.2, which places zinc above iron.

context: Answer the following about the formation and nature of ionic compounds.
stem: Write the electron-dot structures for sodium, oxygen and magnesium.
solution:
Each structure shows only the **valence (outermost) electrons** as dots around the symbol.

- **Sodium**, \(\text{Na}\) (2,8,1) — one valence electron, so **Na** with a single dot beside it.
- **Magnesium**, \(\text{Mg}\) (2,8,2) — two valence electrons, so **Mg** with two dots beside it.
- **Oxygen**, \(\text{O}\) (2,6) — six valence electrons, so **O** surrounded by six dots, drawn as two pairs and two single dots.
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? with Table 3.3 and Figs. 3.5 and 3.6 — a metal atom loses its valence electrons to attain a noble-gas configuration and a non-metal atom gains them, and the oppositely charged ions are then held by strong electrostatic forces.

context: Answer the following about the formation and nature of ionic compounds.
stem: Show the formation of Na₂O and MgO by the transfer of electrons.
solution:
In both cases the metal **gives up** its valence electrons and oxygen **takes** them, and both partners end with a stable octet.

**Sodium oxide, \(\text{Na}_2\text{O}\).** Each sodium atom has one electron to give and oxygen needs two, so **two sodium atoms** are required for one oxygen atom:

\(2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{Na}^+ + 2e^-\)

\(\text{O} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}\)

giving \(2\text{Na}^+ + \text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O}\)

**Magnesium oxide, \(\text{MgO}\).** Magnesium has two electrons to give and oxygen needs exactly two, so they pair **one to one**:

\(\text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+} + 2e^-\)

\(\text{O} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}\)

giving \(\text{Mg}^{2+} + \text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{MgO}\)
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? with Table 3.3 and Figs. 3.5 and 3.6 — a metal atom loses its valence electrons to attain a noble-gas configuration and a non-metal atom gains them, and the oppositely charged ions are then held by strong electrostatic forces.

context: Answer the following about the formation and nature of ionic compounds.
stem: What are the ions present in these compounds?
solution:
- **Sodium oxide, \(\text{Na}_2\text{O}\)** — two sodium ions \(\text{Na}^+\) and one oxide ion \(\text{O}^{2-}\).
- **Magnesium oxide, \(\text{MgO}\)** — one magnesium ion \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) and one oxide ion \(\text{O}^{2-}\).

In each compound the total positive charge balances the total negative charge, so the compound as a whole is neutral.
groundedIn: §3.3 How do Metals and Non-metals React? with Table 3.3 and Figs. 3.5 and 3.6 — a metal atom loses its valence electrons to attain a noble-gas configuration and a non-metal atom gains them, and the oppositely charged ions are then held by strong electrostatic forces.

stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
solution:
An ionic compound is built of **oppositely charged ions packed together and held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction**.

Melting means breaking that rigid arrangement apart so the ions can move. Because the inter-ionic attraction is strong, a **considerable amount of energy** is needed to overcome it — and that energy has to be supplied as heat. Hence the high melting points (and, for the same reason, high boiling points).
groundedIn: §3.3.1 Properties of Ionic Compounds, item (ii) Melting and Boiling points, with Table 3.4 — a considerable amount of energy is required to break the strong inter-ionic attraction.

stem: Mineral
solution:
**A mineral is an element or a compound that occurs naturally in the earth's crust.**

Every ore is a mineral, but most minerals are not ores — the extra condition is in the next definition.
groundedIn: §3.4 Occurrence of Metals and §3.4.2 Enrichment of Ores — minerals are the elements or compounds occurring naturally in the earth's crust, ores are those minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted, and gangue is the soil and sand contaminating a mined ore.

stem: Ore
solution:
**An ore is a mineral that contains a high enough percentage of a particular metal for the metal to be extracted from it profitably.**

The test is economic as much as chemical: a mineral holding a metal in too small a proportion to be worth extracting is not called an ore.
groundedIn: §3.4 Occurrence of Metals and §3.4.2 Enrichment of Ores — minerals are the elements or compounds occurring naturally in the earth's crust, ores are those minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted, and gangue is the soil and sand contaminating a mined ore.

stem: Gangue
solution:
**Gangue is the unwanted impurity — soil, sand and the like — that contaminates an ore as it is mined.**

It must be removed before the metal is extracted. The separation techniques used exploit the differences between the physical or chemical properties of the gangue and of the ore.
groundedIn: §3.4 Occurrence of Metals and §3.4.2 Enrichment of Ores — minerals are the elements or compounds occurring naturally in the earth's crust, ores are those minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted, and gangue is the soil and sand contaminating a mined ore.

stem: Name two metals which are found in nature in the free state.
solution:
**Gold and silver.**

Platinum and copper are equally correct answers. These metals sit at the **bottom of the activity series**, so they are too unreactive to have combined with other elements, and are found uncombined — in the native or free state.
groundedIn: §3.4.1 Extraction of Metals, which records that gold, silver, platinum and copper are found in the free state, and Fig. 3.9, which marks the least reactive metals as found in the native state.

stem: What chemical process is used for obtaining a metal from its oxide?
solution:
**Reduction.** Obtaining a metal from its compound is a reduction process, because the metal ion gains electrons and the oxygen is removed.

Which reducing agent is used depends on where the metal sits in the activity series:

- **Metals in the middle** (zinc, iron, lead) — their oxides are reduced by heating with **carbon**: \(\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)\).
- **Metals at the top** (sodium, magnesium, calcium, aluminium) — carbon cannot reduce their oxides, because these metals have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon does. They are obtained by **electrolytic reduction**.
groundedIn: §3.4.4 Extracting Metals in the Middle of the Activity Series (reduction with carbon) and §3.4.5 Extracting Metals towards the Top of the Activity Series (electrolytic reduction).

context:
Metallic oxides of zinc, magnesium and copper were heated with the following metals.

| Metal → | Zinc | Magnesium | Copper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zinc oxide | | | |
| Magnesium oxide | | | |
| Copper oxide | | | |

(The book prints this grid empty, for the reader to fill in.)
stem: In which cases will you find displacement reactions taking place?
solution:
A metal displaces another metal from its oxide only if it is **more reactive** than that metal. From the activity series, **magnesium \(>\) zinc \(>\) copper**.

Filling the grid — **D** marks a displacement, **N** no reaction:

| Oxide heated with → | Zinc | Magnesium | Copper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zinc oxide | N | **D** | N |
| Magnesium oxide | N | N | N |
| Copper oxide | **D** | **D** | N |

So displacement occurs in **three** cases:

- **Zinc oxide + magnesium**: \(\text{ZnO} + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{Zn}\)
- **Copper oxide + zinc**: \(\text{CuO} + \text{Zn} \rightarrow \text{ZnO} + \text{Cu}\)
- **Copper oxide + magnesium**: \(\text{CuO} + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{MgO} + \text{Cu}\)

Every other cell is no reaction: magnesium oxide cannot be reduced by either of the less reactive metals, and a metal cannot displace itself from its own oxide.
groundedIn: §3.2.5 The Reactivity Series with Table 3.2, which orders Mg above Zn above Cu, read with §3.2.4 — a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

stem: Which metals do not corrode easily?
solution:
**Gold and platinum**, and to a large extent **silver**.

These are the metals at the **bottom of the activity series**. Corrosion is a reaction with the air and moisture around the metal, so the less reactive the metal, the less readily it corrodes — gold and platinum do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures, which is also why they are found in nature in the free state.

Silver does eventually tarnish, turning black as it reacts with the sulphur in the air, but it resists corrosion far better than iron.
groundedIn: §3.5 Corrosion, which lists what happens to silver, copper and iron on exposure to air, read with §3.2.1, where silver and gold are recorded as not reacting with oxygen even at high temperatures.

stem: What are alloys?
solution:
**An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal and a non-metal.**

It is made by melting the primary metal first, dissolving the other elements in it in definite proportions, and then cooling the mixture to room temperature. If one of the metals is **mercury**, the alloy is called an **amalgam**.

Alloying changes a metal's properties for the better — pure iron is soft and stretches when hot, but iron with about 0.05% carbon is hard and strong, and iron with nickel and chromium gives **stainless steel**, which is hard and does not rust.
groundedIn: §3.5.1 Prevention of Corrosion, which defines an alloy, names the amalgam case and gives the iron-carbon and stainless-steel examples.
